summary: Extends Mobile IPv6 so a mobile node may register several care-of addresses at once with its home agent and correspondents, instead of just one primary address, for reasons like cost, bandwidth and delay.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of giving friends just one phone number, you give several so they can use whichever is cheapest or fastest.

questions: what is multiple care-of addresses registration
what is a binding identifier in mobile ipv6
what is bulk registration in mobile ipv6
subtitle: Lets a Mobile IPv6 device register several care-of addresses at once, one per network connection, and keep them all alive.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 lets a mobile node bind only one care-of address to its home address at a time, so a device with several network interfaces cannot use them together while keeping its sessions alive.
tldr.mechanism: The mobile node gives each care-of address a 16-bit Binding Identification number (BID) and sends it in a new Binding Identifier mobility option, so the home agent and correspondent nodes keep one binding cache entry per BID.
tldr.outcome: A device can hold several simultaneous bindings, send them in one bulk Binding Update to its home agent, and even keep its home-link attachment alongside foreign links. RFC 6089 later updated this specification.

today: RFC 5648 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2009, and it has been updated by RFC 6089. Read the two together when implementing it.

sections.title: Introduction: One Home Address, Many Paths
sections.content:
A mobile node often has several network interfaces, such as 802.11, 802.16 or cellular radios. Under Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) it can bind only one care-of address at a time to its home address, so it cannot use all of its interfaces and still keep the session continuity that Mobile IPv6 provides.

This document extends Mobile IPv6 so a node can register multiple care-of addresses for one home address. The reasons it gives are cost, bandwidth and delay. The same extension can be used by mobile routers running the NEMO Basic Support protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone has Wi-Fi and a mobile signal, but the old rules said you could tell the world about only one of them. This RFC lets you share both.

sections.title: Binding Identifiers and Bindings
sections.content:
The key idea is the Binding Identification number (BID). The mobile node generates one BID for each care-of address and stores it in its Binding Update List. The home agent copies the BID into the matching binding cache entry. If a Binding Update arrives with a BID that does not match an existing entry, the home agent MUST create a new entry for that care-of address.

Lookups change too. Where RFC 3775 searched by home address alone, a node now searches by home address plus BID when it knows the BID. For ordinary data packets no BID is carried, so the node uses policy or flow filters if it has them (their design is out of scope). Otherwise it SHOULD use the binding last verified by data or signaling from the mobile node. To avoid trouble for TCP, a single flow, identified by its 5-tuple, SHOULD go to only one care-of address at a time.

The specification is backward compatible. A receiver that does not understand the option skips it and treats the Binding Update as plain RFC 3775. A supporting receiver reflects the option in the Binding Acknowledgement, so a mobile node that sees no option in the reply knows to fall back to legacy behaviour.
sections.plainLanguage: Each of your phone numbers gets a sticker with a number on it. When someone calls, they can tell which line they mean. If a friend ignores the stickers, the old one-number way still works.

sections.title: The Binding Identifier Option and New Status Codes
sections.content:
The extension adds an Overwrite (O) flag to the Binding Update. When set, all existing binding cache entries for the mobile node are replaced by the entries in this update.

The new Binding Identifier mobility option (type 35) carries a 16-bit BID, an 8-bit Status field, an H flag and an optional care-of address. Its Length must be 4 (no address), 8 (an IPv4 care-of address) or 20 (an IPv6 care-of address). A BID of zero is reserved and SHOULD NOT be used. The option may appear in Binding Update, Binding Acknowledgement, Binding Refresh Request, and Care-of Test Init and Care-of Test messages.

The per-BID Status field lets a home agent report a result for one binding inside a bulk registration. The RFC also defines new Binding Acknowledgement status values, listed in the table below.
sections.plainLanguage: The sticker is a small tag attached to each message: a number, an optional address, and a little result box so the answer can say which line worked.

sections.title: What the Mobile Node Does
sections.content:
A mobile node assigns a BID, an integer from 1 to 65535, to each care-of address, unique for a given home address. The first time it registers a BID it MUST include the Care-of Address field. Later refreshes and de-registrations may omit it. A node with several interfaces and a node with one interface and several prefixes are treated the same.

Bulk registration puts a Binding Identifier option for each BID into a single Binding Update, which saves signaling on scarce links. It is supported only for home registration, never with a correspondent node, because the return routability test cannot easily verify several care-of addresses in one message. A correspondent node registration needs both a home and a care-of keygen token, kept for each care-of address.

To remove one binding, the node sends a Binding Update with lifetime zero and the BID. A plain zero-lifetime update without the option deletes every binding. When a node first starts up and registers multiple bindings, it MUST set the O flag, since it may have lost track of old entries at the home agent.

If the acknowledgement carries a status of 128 or more, the node reacts to the code. For example, on MCOA PROHIBITED it MUST stop registering multiple bindings with that node.
sections.plainLanguage: You pick a number for each line, tell your home base about all of them in one note if you like, and cross out one line by saying its number. When you first wake up, you say forget everything I told you before.

sections.title: What the Home Agent and Correspondent Do
sections.content:
A Binding Update without a Binding Identifier option is handled as in RFC 3775, which means it replaces all existing bindings. With the option, the receiver checks the length (a wrong value gets MCOA MALFORMED), and a correspondent node that sees several options rejects the update with MCOA BULK REGISTRATION PROHIBITED.

A zero lifetime deletes just the binding for that BID. Otherwise the receiver registers or updates the binding for the BID. If the O flag is not set and the receiver holds a regular binding with no BID, it does not process the update and replies MCOA NON-MCOA BINDING EXISTS.

When an acknowledgement is requested, the BID options are copied back. A correspondent node always puts its status in the main Status field. A home agent may put a per-BID status in the option, and then sets the main status to MCOA NOTCOMPLETE. Packets that arrive with a Home Address option must have a source address equal to one of the binding's care-of addresses, otherwise they are discarded and a Binding Error is sent.
sections.plainLanguage: The home base keeps one card per sticker number. A new number gets a new card, a known number updates its card, and a note with no sticker wipes the stack and starts over.

sections.title: Returning Home with Several Interfaces
sections.content:
A node that comes back to its home link has two options. It can use only the home-link interface and de-register all bindings with the home agent, while still registering its other care-of addresses with correspondent nodes. Or it can use the home link and the visited links together.

The second option creates a conflict over who defends the home address with Neighbor Discovery. The home agent MUST intercept all traffic for the node. If the home agent is the only router on the home link, the mobile node can defend its address normally. If there are other routers, the mobile node MUST NOT run Neighbor Discovery for the home address, so the home agent keeps proxying. That case is signaled with status MCOA RETURNHOME WO/NDP (5). The node registers a home binding by sending the H flag with the home address as the care-of address, and includes its link-layer address using the option from RFC 5568.

When the node leaves the home link it SHOULD immediately send a Binding Update with the H flag unset, which makes the home agent stop forwarding to the home link.
sections.plainLanguage: If you come home but still have a friend visiting through another door, someone has to decide who answers the doorbell. This part of the RFC says who does it so mail does not get lost.

sections.title: NEMO and Dual Stack Mobile IPv6
sections.content:
Binding management is the same for a mobile host and for a NEMO mobile router, so mobile routers can use the extension as is.

With Dual Stack Mobile IPv6 (RFC 5555) some care-of addresses may be IPv4. The IPv4 address goes in the Binding Identifier option, and the separate IPv4 Care-of Address option MUST be omitted. Bulk registration MUST NOT be used for the first registration from an IPv4 care-of address, because the Binding Update exchange is used to detect a NAT on the path. A node may also request an IPv4 home address, but then the same set of care-of addresses is registered for both home addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The same stickers work for devices that carry a whole network with them, and for lines that use the older kind of address. Old-style lines just need one extra careful check first.

sections.title: IPsec Interaction and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 assumes one primary care-of address and that the IKEv2 security association is based on it. With several addresses the mobile node picks one care-of address for all IKEv2 messages. To switch, it sends a Binding Update with the new address, its BID option and the K bit set, or else re-establishes the IKEv2 security association. For tunneled Home Test Init messages, the home agent MUST accept any of the node's care-of addresses as the source.

Multiple bindings raise the risk of a redirection attack. A malicious mobile node could bind several victims' addresses and have the home agent tunnel traffic to them, and, unlike the single-address case, it can keep a valid address to control the attack. The home agent does not verify that the node really is at a claimed care-of address, and Mobile IPv6 relies on trust between node and home agent. The RFC advises home agents to verify addresses before using them, but leaves the mechanism out of scope. Bulk registration prevents the usual reachability check, so a home agent may reject it, or the node can register each address individually first and use bulk registration only to refresh.
sections.plainLanguage: If a sneaky friend could give your home base a list of addresses that are not really theirs, mail might get sent to people who never asked for it. So the home base should check each address is really theirs, at least once.

viz.caption: BINDING IDENTIFIER MOBILITY OPTION, FIXED PART (RFC 5648, FIGURE 5)

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Option type value for Binding Identifier.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Option length excluding Type and Length: 4, 8 or 20.

fields.name: Binding ID (BID)
fields.desc: 16-bit unsigned binding identifier; zero is reserved.

fields.name: Status
fields.desc: Per-BID status in a Binding Acknowledgement or Care-of Test.

fields.name: H
fields.desc: Simultaneous home and foreign binding flag.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero by the sender, ignored by the receiver.

items.label: MCOA NOTCOMPLETE
items.desc: Bulk registration: some Binding Identifier options were rejected.

items.label: MCOA RETURNHOME WO/NDP
items.desc: Returning home: the mobile node must not use Neighbor Discovery for the home address.

items.label: MCOA MALFORMED
items.desc: The Binding Identifier option was not formatted correctly.

items.label: MCOA NON-MCOA BINDING EXISTS
items.desc: Bootstrapping registration was sent without the O flag set.

items.label: MCOA PROHIBITED
items.desc: Multiple care-of addresses registration is administratively prohibited.

items.label: MCOA UNKOWN COA
items.desc: No care-of address in the option and no record for that BID.

items.label: MCOA BULK REGISTRATION PROHIBITED
items.desc: Bulk registration is not permitted or not supported.

items.label: MCOA SIMULTANEOUS HOME AND FOREIGN PROHIBITED
items.desc: Simultaneous home and foreign attachment is neither supported nor permitted.
